questions.prompt: Which data structure turns "find two numbers in an array that add up to a target" from O(n²) into a single O(n) pass?
distractors: A sorted array with binary search
questions.explanation: For each number, check whether `target - number` is already in the map (O(1) on average), then add the number. Sorting plus two pointers works too, but costs O(n log n).

questions.prompt: What is the technique called where two indices start at opposite ends of a sorted array and move towards each other?
questions.explanation: Each step discards one end, giving O(n): e.g. pair sums in a sorted array, or checking a palindrome. A sliding window also uses two indices, but both move forward to grow and shrink a range.

questions.prompt: Which technique finds the longest substring without repeating characters in O(n), growing a range on the right and shrinking it from the left?
questions.explanation: Each character enters and leaves the window at most once, so the whole scan is linear. A set or last-seen map tells you when to move the left edge.

questions.answer: Caching a function's results by its arguments, so repeated calls (overlapping subproblems) are answered from the cache
distractors: Storing a function's local variables on the heap instead of the stack
Rewriting a recursive function as a loop
Precomputing every possible input before the program starts
questions.explanation: Naive recursive Fibonacci makes exponentially many calls; memoised, each n is computed once, which makes it O(n). It's top-down dynamic programming.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm finds the shortest paths from one node to every other node in a graph whose edge weights are non-negative?
questions.explanation: Dijkstra repeatedly takes the closest unvisited node from a priority queue. BFS gives shortest paths only when every edge has the same weight; Kruskal builds a minimum spanning tree, which is a different problem.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm orders the nodes of a directed acyclic graph so every edge points from an earlier node to a later one, e.g. a build order for dependencies?
questions.explanation: Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes nodes with no incoming edges; a DFS version outputs nodes in reverse post-order. If nodes are left over, the graph has a cycle.

questions.prompt: How many times does this loop run before it finds 7?
questions.explanation: mid = 2 (5, go right), then lo = 3, hi = 5 gives mid = 4 (9, go left), then lo = hi = 3 gives mid = 3, found. Integer division rounds the midpoint down, which is why it doesn't land on 7 at the second step.
LINQ's OrderBy is a stable sort: items with equal keys keep their original order, so Bob stays before Dan and Ann before Cat. `Array.Sort` and `List<T>.Sort` are not stable.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of building a binary heap from n unsorted items with bottom-up heapify?
questions.explanation: Inserting one item at a time costs O(n log n), but sifting down from the last parent upwards is O(n): most nodes are near the bottom and move only a level or two.

questions.prompt: Which tree data structure stores strings one character per level, so all words with a given prefix are found quickly (e.g. for autocomplete)?
questions.explanation: Finding a prefix costs O(length of the prefix), however many words are stored. A hash table can't answer "everything starting with abc" without scanning every key.

Naive recursion recomputes the same subproblems: calls(n) = 1 + calls(n-1) + calls(n-2), giving 1, 1, 3, 5, 9, 15 for n = 0..5. The local function captures `calls` itself (not a copy), and operands are evaluated left to right, so it's read after Fib(5) has finished.

questions.prompt: Which sorting algorithm is O(n log n) even in the worst case and stable, but needs O(n) extra memory?
questions.explanation: Merge sort always halves the input and merges in linear time, using a buffer. Quicksort is O(n²) in its worst case; heapsort is O(n log n) and in place but not stable.
